record.original_question: Given positive integers k and r, does there exist n such that every k-colouring of the symmetric group S_n contains a monochromatic copy of S_r, where a copy of S_r means the set of all r! concatenations of some partition of the symbols into r disjoint words?

evidence.quote: Question 12.1. Given k and r, does there exist n such that whenever the symmetric group Sn is k-coloured there is a monochromatic copy of Sr?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Identify the symmetric group $S_n$ with the set of all permutations of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, regarded as words of length $n$ over the alphabet $\{1,\dots,n\}$ in which every symbol appears exactly once.

Given an integer $r\ge 1$ and $n\ge r$, a copy of $S_r$ inside $S_n$ is defined as follows. Choose a partition of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ into $r$ disjoint nonempty blocks and, for each block, fix a linear ordering of its elements (so each block becomes a word). For every permutation $\sigma\in S_r$ of the $r$ blocks, form the word obtained by concatenating the $r$ block-words in the order $\sigma$. This produces $r!$ permutations in $S_n$, and this set of $r!$ permutations is called a copy of $S_r$.

Question: For all positive integers $k$ and $r$, does there exist a positive integer $n=n(k,r)$ such that, for every coloring $c:S_n\to\{1,2,\dots,k\}$, there is a monochromatic copy of $S_r$ (i.e.\ a copy of $S_r$ all of whose $r!$ elements receive the same color under $c$)?
artifact.status_search_result: A brief web search did not return specific literature addressing this Ramsey-type question on colorings of the symmetric group seeking monochromatic copies of $S_r$ in the described concatenation sense. No clear resolution (positive or negative) was found, so the current status appears unverified.

status_evidence.snippet: Standard Ramsey theory references covering classical edge/vertex colorings; no entry on Ramsey-type results for colorings of S_n with monochromatic copies of S_r.
status_evidence.claim: General Ramsey theory references do not address this specific permutation-group Ramsey question.
